History and Physical (H&P – Super Detailed)

Consult Summary:
32-year-old woman with sudden-onset continuous vertigo, nausea, and bilateral ear buzzing for 2 hours; provisional diagnosis of labyrinthitis, symptomatic treatment started, and advised urgent in-person review.

History:
• Presenting complaint: Sudden dizziness described as “room spinning,” accompanied by nausea and bilateral ear buzzing.  
• Onset & course: Began abruptly ~2 hours prior while making breakfast; symptoms have been constant since onset. Similar but brief episode (~5–10 min) occurred 1 month ago and resolved spontaneously.  
• Provoking/relieving factors: None identified; standing/walking worsens imbalance.  
• Associated symptoms: Unsteady gait due to vertigo; no limb weakness, no ear pain, no ear discharge, no hearing loss, no recent upper-respiratory symptoms, no fever reported, no vomiting yet, no headaches reported.  
• Review of systems:  
  – Neurologic: No focal weakness or sensory loss.  
  – ENT: Tinnitus; denies otalgia, otorrhea, or hearing deficit.  
  – Constitutional: Denies recent infection or fever.  
  – GI: Nausea without vomiting.  
  – Other systems not discussed.

Past Medical History:
• Premature ovarian failure – managed with hormone-replacement therapy (HRT).  
• No other chronic medical or surgical history reported.

Medications:
• Hormone-replacement therapy – dose/route/frequency not documented.  
• New prescription: [Medication name not documented] – one tablet three times daily for 10 days (route not documented).

Allergies:
• No known drug allergies.

Social History:
• Not discussed: no data on smoking, alcohol, occupation, or recreational drugs.

Family History:
• Not discussed.

Physical Examination:
• Not performed during video consult; no vitals available.

Investigations:
• None performed yet. Planned: in-person otoscopic examination, blood pressure measurement, gait assessment.

Assessment & Plan:

Issue 1: Suspected labyrinthitis (acute vestibular dysfunction)
  – Assessment: Acute continuous vertigo with tinnitus and gait unsteadiness, no focal neurologic deficits; presentation consistent with labyrinthitis.  
  – Plan:  
    • Prescribed vestibular suppressive medication (one tablet TID ×10 days).  
    • Arrange urgent face-to-face appointment for full ENT and neurologic examination, vitals, and possible further investigations.  
    • Safety-netting: If new limb weakness, sudden severe headache, or persistent vomiting occurs, attend Emergency Department immediately.

Issue 2: Symptom control / nausea
  – Assessment: Nausea secondary to vertigo.  
  – Plan: Same vestibular suppressive agent expected to reduce nausea; may consider anti-emetic if symptoms worsen at in-person review.

Issue 3: Follow-up and monitoring
  – Plan: Patient to telephone support line to book in-person appointment within next few days.  
  – Prescription sent to Lloyds Pharmacy; patient advised medication can be taken with or without food.  
  – Review after examination or sooner if red-flag symptoms develop.

General plan items:
• Provide patient information on labyrinthitis and vestibular rehabilitation exercises once diagnosis confirmed.  
• Re-evaluate need for further imaging (e.g., MRI) if atypical features arise.
